affected_parts.evidence: The first symptoms of black Sigatoka disease are tiny, chlorotic spots that appear on the bottom (abaxial) surface of the 3rd or 4th open leaf.

summary.value: Tiny chlorotic spots appear on leaf undersides, growing into thin brown streaks limited by leaf veins. Streaks darken with purple tinge and develop into characteristic black streaking. Adjacent tissue appears water-soaked under high humidity.
summary.evidence: The first symptoms of black Sigatoka disease are tiny, chlorotic spots that appear on the bottom (abaxial) surface of the 3rd or 4th open leaf. The spots grow into thin brown streaks that are limited by leaf veins. The color of the streaks becomes darker, sometimes with a purple tinge, and visible on the top (adaxial) surface. The lesions then enlarge, becoming fusiform or elliptical, and darken to give the characteristic black streaking of the leaves. Adjacent tissue often has a water-soaked appearance, especially under conditions of high humidity.

diagnostic_features.value: Black color in young streaks and spots without distinct yellow halo. Conidiophores produced singly or in small groups (2-5) on lower leaf surface. Conidia taper from base to apex with distinct basal scar.
diagnostic_features.evidence: It has black color in the young streaks and spots and lacks the distinct yellow halo that is present in young streaks of yellow Sigatoka. Mycosphaerella fijiensis produces conidiophores in small groups and not in the larger clusters (sporodochia) produced by M. musicola. Also M. fijiensis has basal scars on the conidium and conidiophore at their points of attachment.

look_alikes.evidence: Although the lesions of yellow Sigatoka ( Mycosphaerella musicola ) may look similar, one can distinguish between the yellow and black Sigatokas by examining conidiophore structure
